subject: Cognitive Science
title: Checklists and Decision Quality
description: A short lesson to help you apply Checklists and Decision Quality.

hook.text: When hospitals introduced a simple surgery checklist, complications dropped 36% and deaths dropped 47%.

buildup.text: Atul Gawande showed that experts fail not from ignorance but from forgetting steps under pressure.

discovery.text: Checklists work by offloading memory demands. They free up cognitive resources for judgment and adaptation.

twist.text: Pilots adopted checklists after a deadly crash in 1935. Before that, flying was considered 'too complex to list.'

climax.text: The key insight: good decisions aren't about being smarter. They're about building systems that catch errors.

punchline.text: The checklist doesn't replace expertise—it protects it.

quiz.question: Why do checklists improve expert performance?
options: They prevent forgetting steps under pressure

details.summary: Atul Gawande showed that simple checklists dramatically reduce errors in surgery, aviation, and other complex domains. Checklists externalize memory, enforce consistency, and prevent omission of critical steps.
details.whyItMatters: Checklists counter the limits of human memory and attention. They are among the cheapest, most effective tools for improving high-stakes decision quality.
takeaways: Checklists reduce errors in surgery and aviation significantly
They work by externalizing memory under cognitive load
Resistance to checklists often reflects ego, not evidence

faq.question: How much do surgical checklists actually help?
faq.answer: The WHO surgical safety checklist reduced major complications by 36 percent and deaths by 47 percent in a global study. The improvements came from basic steps like confirming the patient's identity and the surgical site. The power lies in preventing simple, predictable omissions.

faq.question: Why do some professionals resist using checklists?
faq.answer: Checklists feel beneath experts who have trained for years. They imply that skillful professionals might forget basic steps. But that is exactly the point: under pressure, fatigue, or routine, even experts skip steps. Resistance is about professional identity, not evidence of effectiveness.
